questions.question: Explain what soil and topsoil are, and why topsoil is regarded as a non-renewable resource.
questions.expected_answer: Soil: weathered rock particles (sand, silt, clay) plus humus, water, air and organisms; horizons: topsoil (dark, most humus, nutrients, roots), subsoil, weathered rock, bedrock. Topsoil a few cm to tens of cm thick; one cm can take hundreds of years to form, but can be lost in a few storms, so non-renewable on human timescale. Vegetation protects soil (leaves, roots, litter, slowing water and wind); accelerated erosion is human-induced.

questions.question: Describe the types of soil erosion by water and wind.
questions.expected_answer: Splash erosion by raindrops; runoff when rain exceeds infiltration; sheet erosion (thin even layer, hard to see); rill erosion (small channels); gully erosion/dongas (deep channels, headward erosion, cannot be ploughed; KZN, Eastern Cape, Limpopo, Free State). Wind erosion in dry areas with loose fine soil; removes fine fertile particles, dust storms (Northern Cape, North West, western Free State). Factors: rainfall intensity, wind, slope, soil type, plant cover.

questions.question: Explain how agriculture, construction and mining contribute to soil erosion and describe the effects.
questions.expected_answer: Agriculture: clearing, ploughing leaves bare soil, ploughing downslope, overgrazing and trampling, animal paths, burning. Construction: bulldozers clear vegetation, bare sites; impermeable surfaces increase runoff to streams; roads and informal settlements on slopes. Mining: open-cast mines (coal Mpumalanga, iron ore Northern Cape), dumps and tailings, gullies and dust (Witwatersrand). Effects: lower fertility and yields, more fertiliser, abandoned land; siltation of rivers and dams (Welbedacht Dam); dust, damaged roads, lost biodiversity. SA context: Land Acts 1913/1936 overcrowded reserves, so erosion linked to dispossession.
